statements: The chief complaint is two months of persistent left upper-quadrant abdominal pain.
The patient has recurrent vomiting after eating.
The pain worsens with meals.
The pain and vomiting have caused 5 kg weight loss.
The patient’s main concern is a persistent symptomatic gastric process.
The gastric process is not responding to standard H. pylori-directed ulcer therapy.
Salient positive findings point to an organic gastric lesion rather than functional dyspepsia or simple uncomplicated peptic ulcer disease.
She is 65 years old.
She has postprandial pain.
She has repeated vomiting of recently ingested food.
She has weight loss.
She has conjunctival pallor.
Her hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL.
She has positive fecal occult blood testing.
These findings suggest a clinically significant bleeding gastric lesion with possible partial gastric outlet impairment.
Repeat endoscopy showed a large ulcer on the lesser curvature of the antrum.
CT demonstrated focal asymmetric gastric wall thickening along the lesser curvature.
Lack of improvement after clarithromycin-based H. pylori therapy argues against a routine H. pylori-associated benign ulcer as the sole explanation.
Lack of improvement after levofloxacin-based H. pylori therapy argues against a routine H. pylori-associated benign ulcer as the sole explanation.
She is hemodynamically stable.
She has no fever.
She has no night sweats.
These findings make acute infection less likely.
There is no lymphadenopathy.
There is no hepatosplenomegaly.
There is no ascites.
These findings make advanced disseminated lymphoma or widespread metastatic disease less evident clinically.
Advanced disseminated lymphoma or widespread metastatic disease is not excluded.
Her total leukocyte count is normal.
Her differential is normal.
Her absolute eosinophil count is 147/mm3.
These findings argue against eosinophilic gastroenteritis or a systemic eosinophilic disorder.
She denies allergies.
She denies atopy.
These findings further weaken eosinophilic disease.
No skin lesions are reported.
This argues against systemic infiltrative or vasculitic processes with cutaneous manifestations.
The leading differential is gastric adenocarcinoma.
Gastric adenocarcinoma fits her age.
Gastric adenocarcinoma fits her weight loss.
Gastric adenocarcinoma fits her anemia.
Gastric adenocarcinoma fits her occult GI bleeding.
Gastric adenocarcinoma fits her persistent vomiting.
Gastric adenocarcinoma fits the large gastric ulcer on the lesser curvature/antrum.
Gastric adenocarcinoma fits the focal asymmetric wall thickening on CT.
Gastric cancer commonly presents as a malignant-appearing ulcer or focal thickening.
Gastric cancer may be mistaken initially for benign ulcer disease.
A second consideration is primary gastric lymphoma.
Primary gastric lymphoma can present with abdominal pain.
Primary gastric lymphoma can present with weight loss.
Primary gastric lymphoma can present with anemia.
Primary gastric lymphoma can present with ulceration.
Primary gastric lymphoma can present with focal wall thickening.
The absence of lymphadenopathy makes primary gastric lymphoma somewhat less favored than adenocarcinoma.
The absence of B symptoms makes primary gastric lymphoma somewhat less favored than adenocarcinoma.
The absence of bulky diffuse thickening makes primary gastric lymphoma somewhat less favored than adenocarcinoma.
A third possibility is refractory benign peptic ulcer disease.
Refractory benign peptic ulcer disease includes persistent H. pylori infection.
Refractory benign peptic ulcer disease includes NSAID-related ulcer.
The ulcer location could fit refractory benign peptic ulcer disease.
The pain with meals could fit refractory benign peptic ulcer disease.
Failure of two eradication regimens makes a malignant ulcer much more concerning.
Associated weight loss makes a malignant ulcer much more concerning.
Associated anemia makes a malignant ulcer much more concerning.
Positive occult blood makes a malignant ulcer much more concerning.
Focal asymmetric wall thickening makes a malignant ulcer much more concerning.
Eosinophilic gastritis is much less likely.
The available data do not support eosinophilic gastritis clinically.
There is no peripheral eosinophilia.
There is no atopy history.
There is no allergy history.
The imaging and endoscopic picture is more suggestive of a focal malignant ulcerative lesion.

The combination of older age, constitutional weight loss, iron-deficiency-pattern clues from pallor/anemia with occult bleeding, persistent postprandial symptoms, a large lesser-curvature antral ulcer, and focal asymmetric gastric wall thickening most strongly supports gastric adenocarcinoma.
Gastric adenocarcinoma is listed as a high-probability differential diagnosis.
Primary gastric lymphoma is listed as a medium-probability differential diagnosis.
Refractory benign peptic ulcer disease is listed as a low-probability differential diagnosis.
Eosinophilic gastritis is listed as a low-probability differential diagnosis.
The final diagnosis is gastric adenocarcinoma.

clusters.label: test_ordering

clusters.label: examination

clusters.label: differential_generation
